questions.prompt: Two SELECTs run in one PostgreSQL Read Committed transaction. Another transaction commits between them. What is possible?

choices.text: The second SELECT always reads the other transaction before it commits.
The second SELECT can see the newly committed changes.
Both SELECTs must share a transaction-start snapshot.
The first SELECT retroactively changes its returned result.

questions.explanation: Read Committed takes a fresh snapshot for each statement; it does not expose uncommitted changes.

sources.title: Transaction Isolation
sources.claim: PostgreSQL Read Committed SELECT statements use a snapshot at statement start, Repeatable Read uses a transaction snapshot, and Serializable transactions may fail and require retrying the entire transaction.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL Read Committed SELECT is already running when another transaction commits. What does its ordinary snapshot read show?

choices.text: All uncommitted rows from the other transaction.
The newly committed changes immediately replace rows already scanned.
Only rows from transactions that began after this SELECT.
The committed data visible when this statement began.

questions.explanation: Ordinary SELECT visibility uses its statement-start snapshot. A later statement can obtain a newer one.

questions.prompt: An ordinary SELECT is repeated in a PostgreSQL Repeatable Read transaction. What is its snapshot relationship?

choices.text: Each SELECT uses a different snapshot even without local writes.
The snapshot is fixed when the client TCP connection first opened.
The second read must observe every intervening external commit.
The reads share the snapshot established by the first relevant statement.

questions.explanation: Repeatable Read uses a transaction snapshot established at its first non-transaction-control statement. Own changes remain visible.

questions.prompt: Does PostgreSQL Repeatable Read guarantee that every concurrent execution is equivalent to some serial execution?

choices.text: No; Repeatable Read permits reading uncommitted changes.
Yes, because it automatically locks every row that could be read later.
Yes, because a stable read snapshot prevents every anomaly.
No; Serializable provides a stronger guarantee and can reject conflicts.

questions.explanation: A stable snapshot is not full serializability. PostgreSQL Serializable adds conflict detection and may abort a transaction.

questions.prompt: A Serializable transaction fails with a serialization error after computing an inventory decision. What should the retry do?

choices.text: Retry only COMMIT while retaining the stale application decision.
Repeat only the final UPDATE outside any transaction.
Treat failure as proof the original transaction committed successfully.
Retry the whole transaction, recomputing decisions from its new reads.

questions.explanation: A serialization failure invalidates the attempt. Retry its complete logic so reads and decisions belong to the new transaction.

questions.prompt: One transaction holds FOR UPDATE on an inventory row. Which operation normally waits for its row lock?

choices.text: An ordinary snapshot SELECT reading the committed row.
A competing UPDATE targeting that same row.
An ordinary snapshot SELECT that filters on this row exact primary key.
A SELECT reading an unrelated row with a different key.

questions.explanation: The row lock blocks conflicting writers or locking readers. Ordinary snapshot SELECTs are not blocked by the row lock.

sources.title: Explicit Locking
sources.claim: SELECT FOR UPDATE locks selected rows against competing updates and locking reads until transaction end, does not block ordinary snapshot reads, and deadlocks are resolved by aborting a transaction.

questions.prompt: Which PostgreSQL Read Committed claims are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: An ordinary SELECT excludes uncommitted changes from other transactions.
An ordinary SELECT continually refreshes its snapshot while scanning.
A later SELECT can see changes committed after an earlier SELECT.
Every statement in a transaction necessarily shares its first snapshot.
A statement-start snapshot determines ordinary SELECT visibility.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: dirty reads are excluded. B: Incorrect: the statement snapshot stays fixed. C: Correct: each statement can see a newer committed state. D: Incorrect: successive statements can acquire new snapshots. E: Correct: that is the ordinary visibility boundary.

sources.title: Transaction Isolation
sources.claim: At Read Committed, SELECT sees a statement-start snapshot of committed data and successive statements can see different data.

questions.prompt: Which PostgreSQL Repeatable Read claims are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: It guarantees complete serializability for every concurrent workload.
Every SELECT must expose newly committed external rows.
A transaction can see its own earlier modifications.
A stable snapshot alone rules out all serialization anomalies.
Ordinary reads use a stable transaction snapshot.

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect: Serializable is the stronger isolation level. B: Incorrect: later external commits are outside the snapshot. C: Correct: own writes remain visible. D: Incorrect: serialization anomalies can remain. E: Correct: reads share the established transaction view.

sources.title: Transaction Isolation
sources.claim: Repeatable Read uses a stable snapshot and sees own updates, but it can permit serialization anomalies.

questions.prompt: Which serialization-failure responses are sound? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Design the application to handle the possibility of a retry.
Retain every previous read result and retry COMMIT alone.
Retry the complete transaction logic using new reads.
Assume serialization errors prove a permanent schema defect.
Recompute decisions that depended on the failed transaction reads.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: stronger isolation can reject attempts. B: Incorrect: the entire attempt must be retried. C: Correct: establish a fresh consistent attempt. D: Incorrect: normal concurrent conflicts can cause failure. E: Correct: stale decisions must not survive the retry unchanged.

sources.title: Transaction Isolation
sources.claim: Serializable conflicts can abort transactions and applications must retry the entire transaction, including decision logic.

questions.prompt: Which row-locking and deadlock claims are accurate? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A deadlock can cause PostgreSQL to abort one participating transaction.
Consistent lock acquisition order can reduce deadlock risk.
FOR UPDATE prevents every ordinary SELECT from reading that row.
Conflicting row writers can wait until the locking transaction ends.
A row lock is released immediately after SELECT returns its result.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: abort breaks the detected cycle. B: Correct: a shared ordering avoids many cyclic waits. C: Incorrect: ordinary snapshot reads are not blocked. D: Correct: conflicting locks wait for release. E: Incorrect: locks normally persist until transaction end.

sources.claim: SELECT FOR UPDATE locks selected rows against competing updates and locking reads until transaction end, does not block ordinary snapshot reads, and deadlocks are resolved by aborting a transaction.
